step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: BC Registry Services – Corporate Online and OneStop Business Registry
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Conduct a NUANS name search to ensure the proposed corporate name is distinguishable. Submit a Name Reservation Request through the Corporate Online portal or paper Form NR. Pay the prescribed search fee and record the reservation number.
required_dossiers: Proof of name reservation fee payment
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the name is refused or objected to, amend the name request and file an alternative name submission; reapply with revised corporate name within the reservation validity period.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: BC Registrar of Companies – Corporate Online portal
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Complete and submit Form 1 (Incorporation Application) and Form 2 (Notice of Articles) through the Corporate Online service or by mail. Include the company's articles and declaration that the incorporator is authorized to incorporate. Pay the incorporation fee electronically or by certified cheque.
required_dossiers: Notice of Registered Office and Records Office
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the application is queried, submit an amendment or correction via Corporate Online, provide missing consents or lawful declarations, and refile within the registrar's notice period.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Registered Office and Records Office Designation
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: BC Registrar of Companies – Corporate Online
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Maintain a registered office at a physical address within British Columbia and, if required, a records office. File the Notice of Registered Office and Records Office with the Registrar. The address must not be solely a post-office box and must be available during business hours.
required_dossiers: Notice of Registered Office and Records Office
Address consent from the property owner
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the registered office address is invalid or rejected, file an updated Notice with a qualifying physical address and pay the amendment filing fee.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Share Issuance and First Organizational Governance
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Board of Directors of the corporation
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: After receiving the Certificate of Incorporation, the inaugural directors shall formally adopt the first board resolution to ratify share subscriptions, issue share certificates, fix the registered office, and appoint officers. Prepare and maintain the corporate minute book and share register in compliance with the BCBCA.
required_dossiers: Written consents of directors and officers
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If any required consent is missing, execute a written consent and file it in the corporate records; if share conditions are irregular, update the Notice of Articles.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: CRA Business Number and Program Account Registration
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Canada Revenue Agency – Business Registration Online
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Register the corporation with the CRA to obtain a Business Number (BN) and create program accounts for corporate income tax, GST/HST (if applicable), payroll, and import/export as needed. Update corporate information in the CRA portal and authorize officers.
required_dossiers: CRA Business Registration Online submission confirmation
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If CRA registration is delayed or rejected, call the CRA Business Number hotline, verify the legal name and address match the registry records, and refile the registration.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Municipal Business Licence and Regulatory Account Setup
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Local municipal licensing office (e.g., City of Vancouver Business Licensing and Inspections)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Submit a municipal business licence application for the food-processing premise. Pay the applicable licence fee and provide proof of zoning compliance, health approval, and fire safety clearance. Obtain any local food-processing permits required by municipal by-laws.
required_dossiers: CFIA and health inspection confirmation if applicable
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the licence application is queried, submit amended site plans, secure a zoning variance or obtain the missing inspections, and respond to the municipal notice within the stated cure period.

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: Wastewater (to municipal sewer): must meet BC Municipal Wastewater Regulation (BC Reg 330/2013) effluent limits, typically BOD ≤ 45 mg/L, TSS ≤ 45 mg/L, pH 6–9. national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) / Agence du revenu du Canada — federal tax administration for Part I corporate income tax, GST/HST and payroll. Registration is handled through the federal Business Registration Online (BRO) portal, and ongoing compliance is managed in the CRA My Business Account (MyBA) portal. British Columbia administers the separate 7% Provincial Sales Tax (PST) via the BC Ministry of Finance (eTaxBC / PST Account). The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) administers customs, export declarations and the CBSA Assessment and Revenue Management (CARM) portal.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: 1) Incorporate under the Canada Business Corporations Act or the British Columbia Business Corporations Act (BC Corporate Online) — the 9-digit federal Business Number (BN) is then issued automatically by the CRA through BRO for the corporation's income tax account; 2) add the statutory accounts to the BN: GST/HST account (account type RT) once worldwide taxable supplies exceed CAD 30,000 in the preceding four consecutive calendar quarters, or voluntarily from an earlier effective date; payroll account (RP) if employees are hired; import/export account (RM) required before any customs clearance activity; 3) register separately with BC eTaxBC for a PST vendor account before making PST-collectable sales in British Columbia; 4) for a foreign-parented Canadian subsidiary: appoint resident-Canadian directors (at least 25% of the board for a BC corporation), file the initial notice of directors, and submit Form RC1 to add/confirm accounts; the corporation is itself the registered taxpayer and no extra-territorial registration of the foreign parent is required beyond CRA's non-resident carrying-on-business rules.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Entity_Level_Taxation — A business corporation is a separate taxpayer under Part I of the Income Tax Act with no pass-through to shareholders; Canada has no check-the-box classification regime. Canada applies residence-based worldwide taxation (not a territorial regime): the entity's active business income in British Columbia is subject to a combined approximate rate of 27% (federal general rate 15% after the 10% provincial abatement and 13% general reduction, plus BC general corporate rate 12%). A Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) would qualify for the CAD 500,000 small-business limit (federal 9% + BC 2%); a foreign-controlled Canadian corporation is not a CCPC and is taxed at the 27% general rate. Shareholders are separately taxed on dividends under Canada's dividend gross-up and integration mechanism.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: No US-style check-the-box or pass-through election exists for a Canadian business corporation; CRA treats an entity with corporate attributes as a corporation even where a foreign jurisdiction (e.g., a foreign LLC) has elected flow-through status. Available statutory elections relevant to this entity: (i) GST/HST group registration election under Excise Tax Act s. 156, allowing related resident corporations to be treated as a single registrant for GST/HST purposes; (ii) associated-corporation business-limit allocation agreement under Income Tax Act s. 125(3) (CCPCs only); (iii) voluntary GST/HST registration election for a small-supplier exporter in order to claim input tax credits on export inputs (ETA s. 240(2)); (iv) for hybrid-mismatch situations, the Income Tax Act ss. 18.2/18.21 anti-hybrid rules (in force for payments made after 30 June 2022) disallow deduction/non-inclusion outcomes for cross-border arrangements — they contain ordering rules but no elective reclassification of entity status.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Federal GST (Goods and Services Tax — a VAT, creditable at each stage) plus BC Provincial Sales Tax (PST). British Columbia is a non-participating province, so the 15% HST does not apply in BC; the GST rate is 5% and BC PST is a separate single-stage retail sales tax of 7% on taxable goods and services (no broad input-tax credit for PST on business inputs). Export sales are zero-rated for GST and exempt from BC PST where the goods are shipped outside Canada.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 — worldwide taxable (non-zero-rated) supplies made in a calendar quarter plus the three preceding calendar quarters (small-supplier threshold, ETA s. 148). Registration becomes mandatory once the threshold is exceeded and is voluntary below it. There is no GST threshold for a non-resident carrying on business in Canada. BC PST vendor registration is required as soon as PST-collectable sales or imports for sale in BC commence, with an out-of-province vendor rule applying where remote sellers' taxable sales into BC exceed CAD 10,000 annually; an exporter shipping only outside Canada is not a PST vendor if it holds proper export documentation.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: Canada has no national real-time electronic-invoicing clearance or digital-stamping mandate (no continuous transaction controls). GST/HST returns must be filed electronically by registrants with annual taxable revenue above CAD 1 million, and any net remittance exceeding CAD 10,000 must be paid by electronic funds transfer through MyBA; ordinary commercial invoices in accepted formats remain the statutory support. At the border, CBSA's CARM portal is the statutory single-window platform: export declarations (B13A), customs accounting, eManifest pre-arrival data and commercial accounting declarations are filed electronically through CARM or agency EDI/API integrations. A paper-based 'exit' stamp is not required; the export evidence pack is the transactional control for zero-rating purposes.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Canned/aseptic tapioca pearls exported from Canada are zero-rated under Schedule VI, Part V, s. 5 of the Excise Tax Act where the supplier (a) sells the goods under a written contract contemplating export to a destination outside Canada; (b) ships or delivers the goods outside Canada within a reasonable time after the supply (CRA practice generally accepts 60 days for routine ocean freight); (c) retains documentary proof of export; and (d) has no knowledge that the goods will be diverted back into the Canadian market. Offshore services supplied to non-residents (e.g., formulation, toll production or aseptic packaging services for an overseas boba brand) qualify for zero-rating under ETA Schedule VI, Part V, s. 7 where the service is performed outside Canada, or is not in respect of Canadian real property or tangible personal property located in Canada. Domestically, tapioca pearls sold as 'food or beverage for human consumption' may qualify as zero-rated basic groceries under Schedule VI, Part III; however, if the canned product is characterized as a ready-to-drink beverage with added sweeteners, it is taxable at 5% GST and 7% PST in BC — exporters should therefore rely strictly on the export evidence chain rather than product characterization to sustain 0% GST.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: CBSA Export Declaration (Form B13A filed electronically via the Export Reporting System / CARM) for shipments exceeding CAD 2,000 or any controlled goods — include HS 1903 (tapioca pearls and starch-based substitutes), commodity description, weight, value, origin and destination
Bill of Lading or Air Waybill (or Cargo Control Document / Forwarder's Cargo Receipt) evidencing departure from Canada and overseas delivery of the shipment
Commercial Invoice and signed sales contract specifying Incoterms, payment terms and foreign destination (CRA looks to the full chain of commercial documents per GST/HST Memorandum 4.2 'Exports')
Certificate of Origin (e.g., CPTPP or Canada-Chile preference claim) where the foreign buyer or the Canadian exporter requests preferential tariff treatment at destination

Freight forwarder evidence of arrival and delivery overseas, together with the SWIFT/telegraphic-transfer inward payment receipt or letter-of-credit settlement confirmation evidencing remittance of export proceeds
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: CRA scrutinizes export zero-rating claims on the principle that documentary proof must exist at the time of supply. Where the s. 5 (Schedule VI, Part V) conditions are not met, or goods are diverted to the Canadian market, CRA reassesses the supply as taxable at 5% GST, assesses uncollected tax on the exporter (which is commercially unrecoverable from the foreign buyer), and adds daily compound interest under ETA s. 280 and late-filing/remittance penalties. False statements or omissions in a GST/HST return, made knowingly or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, attract a penalty of the greater of CAD 250 and 5% of the tax or refund misstated (ETA s. 285). Criminal tax evasion under ETA s. 326 (and ITA s. 239) carries a fine of not less than 50% and not more than 200% of the tax sought to be evaded and imprisonment of up to five years on indictment. CBSA enforcement may also impose administrative monetary penalties for false export declarations. While Canada imposes no statutory deadline for repatriation of export proceeds, the 180-day benchmark is the conservative compliance window given the SWIFT LC / TT payment rails used by this entity; receipts materially beyond that period should be documented as genuine trade credit granted under a written agreement to avoid shareholder-benefit or presumed-service recharacterization. Related-party export pricing will additionally attract transfer-pricing review under ITA s. 247, with a 10% penalty where the net adjustment exceeds the lesser of 10% of gross revenue and CAD 5 million.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada) established under the Bank of Canada Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. B-2), administered in conjunction with the Minister of Finance for monetary policy and currency issuance. Banking operations and foreign-exchange dealing are supervised by the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) under the Bank Act (S.C. 1991, c. 46) and the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions Act. Cross-border financial transaction reporting is administered by the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC) under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (PCMLTFA). Canada maintains no dedicated foreign exchange control law and imposes no exchange-control permit regime.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: Canada has full convertibility for both the current and capital accounts under Article VIII of the International Monetary Fund Articles of Agreement. The Currency Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. C-52) and the Bank of Canada Act impose no restriction on the acquisition, holding, conversion, or repatriation of foreign currency or CAD. The Canadian dollar (CAD) floats freely; the Bank of Canada's intervention capability is limited and no fixed parity is maintained. Profit remittance, dividend distribution, interest, royalties, management fees, and shareholder loan repayments may be paid to non-residents freely in any currency, subject only to Part XIII non-resident withholding tax under the Income Tax Act and to FINTRAC reporting for electronic funds transfers (EFTs) of CAD 10,000 or more (or foreign equivalent). No statutory approval from OSFI, the Bank of Canada, or the CRA is required for capital repatriation; no black-market premium or dual-exchange-rate mechanism exists.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: None. Canada does not impose a surrender, repatriation, or conversion timeline for export proceeds. Exporters of canned boba tapioca pearls may retain export receivables in USD, CNY, or any freely convertible currency in any domicile without obligation to convert to CAD or to bring funds into Canada. The sole reporting obligation is the FINTRAC EFT cross-border report for the transfer of CAD 10,000 or more, which is automatically filed by the remitting or receiving financial institution; no exporter self-filing is required. Foreign exchange transactions at Canadian banks must be executed at a commercially reasonable market rate, subject to the Federal Retail Payment Activities Act (R.S.C., 2021, c. 8) where applicable to payment service providers, but no centralized conversion rate or surrender ratio exists.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.bank_name: Royal Bank of Canada (RBC Royal Bank)

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Medium — supplementary rail only, primary account prohibited. Foreign digital EMIs (e.g., Wise Business, Airwallex, Payoneer) are not recognized as banks under the Bank Act and are legally barred from accepting Canadian deposits unless authorized as a bank under the Bank Act or licensed as a money service business (MSB) under PCMLTFA and registered with FINTRAC. Since September 2024, the Retail Payment Activities Act (RPAA) administered by the Bank of Canada requires any payment service provider that holds, uses, or directs funds in a retail payment function — including foreign EMIs processing payments for Canadian users — to register with the Bank of Canada; operating without registration is an offense. An overseas EMI may not issue a Canadian-domiciled bank account number, may not participate in Lynx or Payments Canada clearing, and may not serve as the account of record for tax remittance, payroll, CRA payments, or letter-of-credit issuance. Use a Schedule I bank (Big Five) as the primary treasury and clearing house; use EMIs exclusively as an auxiliary low-value disbursement channel for suppliers in mainland China or Southeast Asia that do not require LC documentary settlement.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: In-person attendance by at least one director or authorized signatory is the operational default for tier-1 Canadian banks under PCMLTFA Customer Due Diligence obligations. The bank must verify the identity of all directors, all authorized signing officers, and every beneficial owner holding 25% or more of the shares or voting control. A BC-based branch in Vancouver or Richmond will require a physical KYC/onboarding interview with the designated commercial banking officer; remote opening is only available through each bank's expedited corporate-remote program (e.g., RBC Remote Corporate Onboarding, TD Virtual Account Opening) and is contingent on (i) a low-risk industry classification (ISIC 1030 food manufacturing qualifies), (ii) real-time video verification of the director's government ID, and (iii) subsequent in-branch signing of the banking mandate and deposit account agreement within a defined period. Practical recommendation: schedule a single in-person closing at the Vancouver Trade & Commercial Banking Centre of the chosen bank, attended by the director or corporate secretary; bring the complete incorporation and licensing binder listed in the AML defense section.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: UBO identification threshold under PCMLTFA — foreign holding company or Asia-resident natural person owns 25%+ of BC Corporation; complex multi-tier chain may be flagged during the bank's Politically Exposed Persons (PEP) and sanctions risk screening
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Certified copy of BC Registries Corporate Online extract showing issued share classes and registered holders; notarized subordinate share register; sworn UBO declaration by each ultimate natural-person owner; notarized passport copies of all UBOs; certificate of incumbency and certificate of good standing of the foreign immediate parent; legal opinion from a BC solicitor confirming the corporate chain and absence of nominee holdings; letters of reference from the foreign shareholder's existing bank.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Source of Funds (SoF) / Source of Wealth (SoW) for inbound equity injection or shareholder loan — bank requires clear documentary trail linking funds to the sender and legitimate origin
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Board resolution authorizing share issuance or shareholder loan; signed shareholder loan agreement with commercial terms; 12-month bank statements of the investing shareholder; audited or reviewed financial statements of the parent entity; tax clearance or tax reference letter from the remitter's tax authority; gift deed or share-sale agreement if the transfer derives from an asset disposition; completed bank SoW questionnaire.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Statutory licence verification — canned boba tapioca pearl manufacturing requires a Safe Food for Canadians Act (SFCR) licence from the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) and a municipal business licence; bank onboarding will fail if licensing is incomplete or where the business premises cannot be confirmed
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: SFCR licence number and certificate with the CFIA establishment code; municipal business licence from the applicable BC municipality (e.g., City of Richmond or City of Vancouver); preventive control plan (PCP) summary under SFCR Part 2; lease agreement or property title for the manufacturing facility; utility bill or fire-disaster endorsement evidencing physical premises; product liability insurance certificate.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Counterparty sanctions and supply-chain review — tapioca starch and canning inputs sourced from PRC or Taiwan; bank screens all proposed trade counterparties for OFAC, UN Security Council, and Global Affairs Canada sanctioned lists under the Special Economic Measures Act and the Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Completed bank counterparty questionnaire enumerating all suppliers, customers, and intermediaries; certificate that no counterparty appears on OFAC SDN, EU consolidated, UN 1267/1988, or SEMA lists; export/import customs entries (Canada Border Services Agency B3 or ACI eManifest) for starch, cans, and machinery; supplier registration certificates and incoterms in the purchase orders; attestation of no dual-use or agricultural-sanctions concern.

For the boba/tapioca facility select NAICS 311999 or 311920? Wait NAICS 311999 all other miscellaneous food manufacturing. The target says NAICS 2022 code 311999. So instruct.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident corporation with a Canadian permanent establishment must complete this part and identify the branch/PE address; no foreign address shortcut
Only Canadian-source revenue attributable to the Canadian PE is included; foreign-source revenue excluded

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Taxable income after all deductions including COGS, SG&A and capital cost allowance
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Compute Part I taxable income as if non-resident's Canadian PE were a separate branch; use s. 115 allocation rules

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Federal and British Columbia provincial tax calculation: allocate taxable income to BC permanent establishment through Schedule 4/5, multiply by federal 15% and BC 12% (or SBD rates as applicable)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For treaty-exempt non-residents, no return is required unless a PE exists in Canada; if PE, file T2 and calculate BC tax on PE income under method agreed in treaty

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Capital gains schedule, loss carryforward/carryback application, and related-party transactions with shareholders; include intercorporate dividends and debt financing relevant to boba parent group
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident shareholders must report deemed dispositions/loss? Actually Schedule 13 needs disclose transactions with shareholders including distribution/loans; direct on Form T1134 for foreign affiliate if issued

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late T2 filing: 5% of unpaid balance + 1% per full month of unpaid tax (max 12 months); second offence within three years increases to 10% + 2% per month; late payment interest/criminal prosecution for wilful tax evasion under ITA s. 239
